title: All California Cannabis Clubs Face Closing -- "We’re Going To Stay Here Until The Tanks Come" Vows Peron

content_html_sanitized:
The California state Supreme Court cleared the way Wednesday for closure of medical marijuana clubs in California, by leaving intact a lower-court ruling that the clubs can’t sell the marijuana despite Prop 215 passed in 1996. The appellate ruling is now binding on trial courts statewide, meaning that all clubs can be closed.

The court unanimously denied review of a December appellate decision that said Proposition 215 did not allow anyone to sell marijuana and did not allow a commercial enterprise to furnish marijuana as a marijuana as a "primary caregiver." See Full Text of Proposition 215 Compassionate Use Act of 1996

The 1st District Court of Appeal ruled in December that state law prohibits anyone, including a nonprofit organization, from selling marijuana or possessing it for sale. Presiding Justice J. Clinton Peterson said the only way a patient can obtain marijuana legally is to grow it or obtain it from a primary caregiver who has grown it. A primary caregiver cannot be a commercial enterprise like a club, Peterson said.

In effect the courts have ruled that a "primary caregiver" has to be an individual even though Prop 215 had no such provision and there are many other situations in which a primary caregiver may be a commercial institution.

As usual, Dennis Peron is defiant. "We’re going to stay here until the tanks come," he vowed. "It may be against the law to sell marijuana but it’s morally wrong to let someone die, and we are saving lives here."

"Voters did not intend to allow commercial enterprises to sell narcotics, like Mr. Peron’s doing," said John Gordnier, a senior assistant attorney general. Only non-profit organizations like pharmaceutical companies and drug stores are allowed to do that!

Federal prosecutors have also asked a federal judge to shut down Peron’s club and five others in Northern California, saying they are violating federal law against the possession and sale of marijuana, regardless of Proposition 215. This state ruling will presumably put the state ahead of the feds and give Dan Lungren the pleasure of inflicting further pain and suffering on the sick and dying. He believes that this is the best way to get the Republican nomination for governor.

This action is a humanitarian disaster, but it will have the effect of forcing the issue of supplying marijuana to a wide variety of patients for whom the individual grower, whether the patient himself, or "primary caregiver," is not a viable option.

Examples of this would include:

  1. A person in the midst of chemotherapy discovers that the pharmaceutical anti-emetics no longer work, or are simply unaffordable. They are terribly expensive.


  2. See     Costs keeping 'rescue' drugs from patients  

  3. People living on the margin. Chronic and terminal illness can be very disruptive to someone’s life. Damned inconvenient. Peron’s club serves many such people.

  5. Many people do not even have a place where they can smoke, much less grow marijuana.

  6. Many people do not have any home or family, much less a primary caregiver.

  7. Ironically, there are people at the other end of the social scale who may find this equally impossible. For example, a family with several children, living in a small town with a seemingly idyllic middle class existence. For them growing marijuana would entail substantial problems and legal risks.


  8. See     My Problem and how I solved it, "I broke the law to save my son."

For both the comfortable suburbanite or any "primary caregiver," there is one little catch to this "grow-your-own" solution. It violates federal law and would make the grower subject to felony prosecutions and allow the government to seize their home. Freedom’s just another word for nothing left to lose.
